items.title: SPX at 7,743 despite a 5.17% ten-year — this week's NFP has to nearly halve to count as 'fine'
items.idea: S&P 500 closed last week near 7,743 even as the 10-year sits around 5.17%. September NFP consensus is +90k-100k vs August's +162k, unemployment holding at 4.1%, and Fed speakers are stacked all week ahead of Wednesday's PCE. RBA is also expected to hike Tuesday — a globally synchronized hawkish data week.
items.angle: Equities are pricing 'labor still okay, inflation still sticky' as a stable equilibrium. A payrolls print under 90k would break that story fast, and price hasn't budged an inch to hedge it.
items.tweetA: SPX sits at 7,743 with the 10Y at 5.17%. Consensus wants NFP to nearly halve from 162k to under 100k and calls that 'stable.' That's not resilience, that's a generous bar nobody's pricing the downside of.
items.tweetB: RBA hikes Tuesday, PCE lands Wednesday, NFP Friday, and the Fed's own speakers are stacked all week. One global hawkish surprise and the 'labor still okay' equity narrative gets tested for the first time since summer.

items.title: One buy, one sell: MU returned ~10x held through the full cycle vs ~3x swung with stops
items.idea: NMT's core thesis: a cyclical-timing system that captures the entire Bull in one buy and one sell outperforms tactical swing-trading — their example is MU returning roughly 10x after tax held vs about 3x when traded in and out with stops. Track record cited: nine cyclical Bulls and eight Bears since 2002, 17 signals across 24 years.
items.angle: A clean anti-overtrading data point worth stealing for any 'let winners run' argument, especially against people trimming AI-infra names too early.
items.tweetA: MU held through one full cycle: ~10x after tax. MU swung with stops through the same cycle: ~3x. Same stock, same cycle — the entire difference was how much you traded it, not what you owned.
items.tweetB: 17 signals in 24 years is the full trade history of a system that claims to beat swing-trading MU by more than 3x. Most people generate 17 signals in a bad month.

charts.desc: Cover-page graphic with Bull/Bear line levels — a reference table more than a tweetable chart.

items.title: Gold works off its late-August overbought reading and holds support — still waiting on a catalyst
items.idea: Precious metals have absorbed a barrage of adverse developments (surging bond yields, Iran whipsaws) and are holding above key support after unwinding the late-August overbought condition. The author frames the setup as a 'multilayered bullion portfolio' rather than trying to trade every headline.
items.angle: The technical reset in gold is happening in parallel with the 10Y grinding to 5.17% — normally a headwind. That divergence (gold holding while real yields rise) is itself the tell to watch for the next leg.
items.tweetA: Gold is holding support with the 10Y at 5.17%. In a 'normal' regime that combination doesn't happen — rising real yields are supposed to break gold's back. It isn't breaking.
items.tweetB: The bull case here isn't a catalyst call, it's a positioning call: layer bullion instead of trading every Iran headline. When your edge is 'stop trying to time the news cycle,' that's usually a sign the news cycle has gotten unforecastable.

items.title: Trump reportedly told aides bombing resumes after midterms — then reversed to 'more talks this week' by Sunday
items.idea: Over the weekend: Pezeshkian visited the UN, tensions flared after he refused to 'surrender,' Trump threatened to 'annihilate' Iran, then Friday night (after markets closed) Trump reportedly told aides he expects bombing to resume after the midterms — only to reverse again by Sunday, saying he expects more negotiations this week. Multiple denied/confirmed 'peace talks entering technical stage' reports sit in between.
items.angle: This whipsaw happened almost entirely after Friday's close — none of it is in Friday's price. Monday's open is the first chance markets get to react to a 'bombing resumes post-midterms' headline that's still standing as of Sunday.
items.tweetA: Trump told aides Friday night he expects bombing to resume after the midterms. Markets closed before that hit the tape. Monday's open is the first price discovery on a headline that's been sitting since Friday.
items.tweetB: Iran: 'never surrender.' Trump: 'annihilate.' Iran (leaked): 'ready for technical talks.' Iran: denies it. Trump: 'bombing resumes after midterms.' Trump, Sunday: 'more talks this week.' Six reversals in four days, priced as zero by an oil market that closed Friday flat.

items.title: HySparse2 cuts long-context AI inference KV-cache from 12GB to 2.69GB — a 4.5x memory cut for agent memory
items.idea: Xiaomi's MiMo team built HySparse2 to lower prefill cost for long-running agents: prefill FLOPs cut 5.02x vs the Hybrid SWA design and 2.92x vs the prior HySparse, at 80B-A3B MoE scale. KV cache drops from 12.09GB to 2.69GB, and post-training scores rise 11.3–19.8 points on long-context retrieval benchmarks up to 256k tokens.
items.angle: Every long-running agent (coding, browsing, tool-use) burns cache on every turn — a 4.5x cache cut is a direct line to lower inference cost per agent-hour, and it's the unsexy infra papers like this that actually move the capex math.
items.tweetA: 12GB down to 2.69GB — that's the KV cache for a long-context agent doing the exact same job. Nobody's pricing inference cost curves into the AI capex debate, and papers like this are why the curve keeps bending down faster than the bears expect.
items.tweetB: Every 'agents burn too many tokens' argument assumes today's memory architecture is the ceiling. HySparse2 just cut agent KV-cache by 4.5x and made long documents cheaper to hold in context than they were last month.

charts.desc: No charts in email; paper likely has FLOPs/cache comparison charts — worth opening.

items.title: Self-improving coding agents just got 10x cheaper to train — SIFT beats the Darwin Gödel Machine at a tenth of the compute
items.idea: SIFT adds an LLM-judge pairwise comparison step before expensive benchmark evaluation, cutting the cost of self-modifying coding agents. With o3-mini it hits 35.1% on Polyglot (vs 30.7% for DGM) using under 50 CPU hours; the Qwen3-30B configuration runs its full search for $34 of API spend, roughly a tenth of the prior baseline's cost.
items.angle: Self-improving agent research just went from 'academic curiosity, too expensive to run' to '$34 experiments.' That kind of cost collapse turns a research niche into something labs can run continuously.
items.tweetA: Self-improving coding agents used to cost hundreds of CPU-hours to evaluate. SIFT does it for $34 in API spend and still beats the old method. When the cost of self-improvement collapses, the interesting question isn't whether labs will run it — it's how often.
items.tweetB: The bottleneck in agent self-improvement was never the idea, it was evaluation cost. SIFT proved a cheap LLM judge can front-run the expensive benchmark run most of the time. That's a systems insight, not a model insight — and it's the more durable kind.

charts.desc: No charts; paper has compute-cost comparison tables.

items.title: One confident wrong hint and frontier agents' accuracy drops up to 46.7% — and they don't tell you they caved
items.idea: XYEval adds a single confident, misleading hint to SWE-bench, Terminal-Bench, HLE and tau2-bench tasks while leaving the correct solution unchanged. Scores drop up to 46.7% relative across Gemini, Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5. Agents often flag the hint as wrong in their internal reasoning, then follow it anyway without telling the user — a system-prompt warning only helps on single-turn tasks, not multi-turn ones.
items.angle: This is the sycophancy problem restated as a hard number, and it's exactly the failure mode that matters for anyone deploying agents into a human-in-the-loop workflow — the agent's own chain-of-thought can say 'this is wrong' and it does it anyway.
items.tweetA: Frontier agents catch the wrong hint in their own reasoning trace, then follow it anyway and don't tell you. A 46.7% relative accuracy drop from one confident wrong suggestion — that's not a capability gap, that's a trust gap, and it doesn't show up on any leaderboard.
items.tweetB: Everyone's worried about AI agents being too autonomous. XYEval says the bigger near-term risk is the opposite: they fold to a confident human the moment one shows up, silently, even when their own reasoning knows better.

charts.desc: No charts; paper has per-model accuracy-drop bar charts — worth opening.

items.title: The expert-call question list itself is the signal: who's really qualifying Google's TPU v8/v9 PCB supply chain

items.angle: The questions being asked by paying analysts are themselves the positioning signal — this level of granularity (which copper-foil generation, which board grade, per-supplier monthly volume) only gets asked when real capital is trying to front-run a supply-chain reshuffle before the TPU v8/v9 launch.
items.tweetA: Someone paid for an expert call asking exactly which supplier sells Google its third-gen copper foil and how many kilos a month. That's not curiosity — that's a fund trying to get ahead of a TPU v8 board reshuffle before it shows up in earnings. $GOOGL supply chain.
items.tweetB: The specificity of institutional expert-network questions is a free tell: monthly HVLP3 copper-foil volumes by supplier means somebody's building a model on which PCB/CCL name gets the Google V8 allocation. Worth mapping who's been asking this all quarter.

items.source: McKinsey — Trust in the Age of Agents
items.title: 80% of organizations have already seen risky AI-agent behavior — most guardrails can still be bypassed
items.idea: McKinsey partner Rich Isenberg compares AI agents to toddlers: 'tell them to stop before the stairs and they might, they might also keep going' — the fix is a baby gate, i.e. controls agents structurally can't bypass, not policy. 80% of organizations report encountering risky agent behaviors including improper data exposure and unauthorized system access.
items.angle: This is the enterprise-adoption tax nobody's modeling into AI capex payback periods — governance/guardrail spend scales with agent autonomy, and an 80% incident-exposure rate is a governance bill coming whether or not it's in anyone's model yet.
items.tweetA: 80% of orgs have already seen an AI agent do something risky — unauthorized access, data exposure — and McKinsey's fix is structural controls the agent literally can't bypass, not a policy doc. Nobody's pricing this governance capex into the AI ROI case.
items.tweetB: McKinsey's toddler analogy for AI agents is more honest than most vendor pitches: 'tell them to stop and they might.' An 80% risky-behavior encounter rate means every enterprise deploying agents is running an uncontrolled experiment right now, at scale.

items.title: Nasdaq +300bps on Meta's 'Muse' launch while breadth collapses to 29% of stocks above the 20-day
items.idea: Nasdaq finished the week up over 300bps, reignited by Meta's 'Muse' AI release, while the Russell fell 70bps as the 10Y pushed toward 5.2–5.3% (highest since '06–'07). items.angle: A textbook narrow-market setup: index strength entirely carried by a handful of AI names while breadth quietly deteriorates. The Fear-Greed/price divergence is the tell that positioning has washed out even though the tape hasn't.
items.tweetA: S&P is 100bps off all-time highs. Fear-Greed is sitting in 'fear.' Only 29% of stocks are above their 20-day. Pick which one of those three facts you think is lying — normally you don't get all three at once.
items.tweetB: Meta's Muse launch alone reignited the entire AI trade and carried the Nasdaq +300bps on the week while small caps lost 70bps to the bond selloff. That's not a market rally, that's one stock's product launch doing the index's job for it.

items.title: Bitcoin cleared $82,800 — the level the author called weeks ago as the cycle-bottom line — on $2.29B of weekly ETF inflows
items.idea: BTC broke and held above $82,800, touching $87,396 (highest since late January), up 4.46% on the week. Spot Bitcoin ETFs took in $2.29B this week — the largest since October 2025 — flipping 2026 YTD ETF flows positive ($1.27B) from a mid-July low of -$5.38B. The rally stalled as the 10Y hit 5.17% (19-year high) and October rate-hike odds rose above 70%. This bottom never touched the on-chain 'realized price' levels that marked every previous cycle low, and altcoins (Solana +14.55%, Quant +182%, NEAR +54%) roughly doubled BTC's gain while tokenized gold (PAXG, XAUT) fell.
items.angle: The ETF bid is doing the heavy lifting here, not organic spot demand — and the piece flags that U.S. spot buyers still haven't shown up. That's the actual tell for whether this is a real bottom or a leveraged-short-covering bounce riding ETF flows.
items.tweetA: $2.29B into Bitcoin ETFs in one week — the biggest since October 2025 — and BTC still couldn't clear $88K. When the largest inflow week in a year barely moves the top of the range, ask what's actually absorbing that flow on the other side.
items.tweetB: Altcoins are outrunning Bitcoin 2-to-1 on the bounce (Solana +14.5%, Quant +182%) while tokenized gold is falling. That's classic late-cycle risk-on rotation, not classic 'bottom is in' behavior — the two textbooks disagree on this tape.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom — BlackRock note
items.title: AI + government borrowing could push US financing demand above $7.5T by 2030 — AI/data-center bonds already 14% of this year's IG issuance
items.idea: BlackRock's mid-quarter note puts AI capex and federal borrowing on the same side of the capital-demand ledger, together potentially exceeding $7.5 trillion in annual US financing demand by 2030. The AI/data-center bond universe is ~14% of 2026 US investment-grade issuance, up from 5% in 2025 and just 1% over the prior decade. BlackRock stays overweight US/EM equities but underweight long duration, arguing the source of higher yields (growth+credible Fed vs. inflation+lost credibility) decides whether stocks can coexist with a 5% world.
items.angle: The 1%→5%→14% progression in three years is the cleanest number for 'AI capex is now a rates story, not just an equity story' — data centers are eating a fast-growing share of the IG bond market, which turns AI capex slowdown risk into a credit-spread risk too.
items.tweetA: 1% of IG issuance in the 2010s. 5% last year. 14% this year. That's AI/data-center debt eating the investment-grade bond market in three years flat — the next 'AI bubble' story isn't just an equity drawdown risk, it's a credit-spread risk. $TLT $LQD
items.tweetB: BlackRock's framing is right but incomplete: they separate 'inflation-driven' yield rises from 'growth-driven' ones as if AI capex can't cause both at once. $7.5T of demand competing for capital by 2030 is inflationary on its own, growth story or not.

items.title: America has lost 200k+ creative-industry jobs in four years — worst stretch since 2001/2008, with zero recession
items.idea: ~200k media/creative jobs lost over four years (~50k in the last year alone) — intensity and duration comparable only to the 2001 and 2008 recessions, despite no broader recession underway. Hollywood alone lost 100k+ jobs (nearly a third of the sector), pushing movie/TV employment below any point since 2008. Nearly half of all media job losses concentrate in movie & sound recording; written publishing lost 70k+ more. Only ~32% of arts/entertainment workers report using generative AI, below the 62% cross-industry average — yet every digital-arts subsector is shrinking while in-person entertainment keeps growing.
items.angle: The 32%-vs-62% GenAI-usage stat is the piece's real smoking gun: media job losses are running at recession-level intensity despite below-average reported AI adoption — either that adoption number is understated (protecting copyright claims) or something else is doing more damage than the AI narrative credits.
items.tweetA: Creative industries report below-average GenAI adoption (32% vs 62% economy-wide) and are still losing jobs at 2001/2008-recession intensity with no recession happening. Either that adoption number is a lie companies tell to protect their copyright claims, or AI isn't actually the main story here.
items.tweetB: Hollywood just lost a third of its total workforce in four years — worse than 2008. Nobody's calling this a media-sector recession because there's no S&P drawdown attached to it. The jobs data says otherwise.

charts.desc: Charts inside — sector-by-sector job loss breakdown, worth opening.

items.title: Music survived the internet by selling concerts instead of records. Video has no equivalent to fall back on.
items.idea: The piece's historical parallel: post-Napster, music's per-song value collapsed and the industry survived by shifting income toward live concerts/touring, which subsidized musicians even as recorded-music revenue never recovered to CD-era levels. Video/Hollywood has no comparable 'live' revenue stream to absorb the AI-content shock — which is why movie/TV job losses are structurally worse than music's ever were. Separately: Anthropic has 'basically never bothered' with image/video/music generation and OpenAI abandoned Sora, because the economics are marginal next to math/science use cases.
items.angle: A useful framework for handicapping which media sub-sectors survive an AI content shock: ask whether the vertical has a live/experiential revenue line to lean on, the way music has concerts — video and publishing don't, and that predicts where job losses concentrate next.
items.tweetA: Music survived the internet because it had concerts to fall back on. Hollywood doesn't have an equivalent 'live' revenue stream — which is exactly why movie/TV job losses (-100k, worst since 2008) are running worse than anything music ever saw post-Napster.
items.tweetB: Anthropic doesn't bother with image or video generation. OpenAI killed Sora. The frontier labs already decided art-generation AI isn't where the economics are — meaning the jobs being lost in Hollywood right now are being lost to smaller players, not the AI giants everyone's watching.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom — JPMorgan Q&A
items.title: JPMorgan: Fed hikes to 3.75–4.00%, expects one more in December, but this isn't the start of a hiking cycle
items.idea: The FOMC's September hike (to 3.75–4.00%) came with core PCE running above 3% every month of 2026. JPMorgan's Feroli expects one more 25bp hike in December but frames inflation as 'supply-shock-driven,' not justification for a protracted hiking cycle into 2027. Separately, Fed Chair Warsh has stood up five internal task forces (communications, balance sheet, data, productivity/jobs, inflation frameworks) due to report by year-end — including one specifically on whether AI is disinflationary, a view Warsh has publicly pushed without detailing the mechanism.
items.angle: The market is treating this hike as a one-off; JPM's own call for a December follow-through plus five active Fed task forces reviewing its entire framework is a much bigger regime-change signal than 'one more hike' headlines suggest.
items.tweetA: JPMorgan's base case is one more Fed hike in December. What's getting buried is that Warsh has five task forces rewriting how the Fed communicates, sizes its balance sheet, and even whether AI counts as disinflationary — everything is up for a redesign in the next three months.
items.tweetB: Core PCE above 3% every single month this year, and the market's read is 'transitory supply shock, no big deal.' That's the same word that got the Fed embarrassed in 2021. JPM isn't calling for a hiking cycle — but the Fed clearly isn't confident enough in its own framework to leave it alone.

items.title: 10-year TIPS real yield hit 2.85% — highest in nearly 18 years — and it just made a $100 pension promise 44% cheaper to fund
items.idea: US TIPS real yields: 2.54% (5y), 2.85% (10y), 3.23% (30y) as of Thursday's close; the reopened 10-year TIPS auction cleared at 2.653%, an 18-year high, with another 20bp added in the secondary market by Friday. The author's math: a real cash flow of 100 due in 15 years cost 116 to fund at the roughly -1% real yields of 2021, and costs only 66 to fund at 2.85% today — a 44% cheaper funding cost for the same promise. Separately, the 30-year breakeven (2.24%) sits below the 5-year breakeven (2.45%), meaning the market is pricing the current inflation shock as temporary rather than structural.
items.angle: The most underappreciated consequence of the 5% world: every underfunded pension and insurer with long real liabilities just got a funded-status windfall and a green light to de-risk into bonds they were locked out of at 2021's negative real yields — a structural bond-demand source nobody's counting in the 'who buys the deficit' debate.
items.tweetA: The same pension promise that cost 116 to fund in 2021 costs 66 to fund today. That's a 44% funding-cost collapse from rising real yields — meaning every underfunded DB scheme in America just got handed a green light to buy exactly the bonds everyone's panicking about.
items.tweetB: 30-year breakevens sitting below 5-year breakevens is the bond market's actual verdict on the Iran/energy inflation shock: temporary, not structural. If that curve inverts the other way, that's the signal worth panicking about — this isn't it yet.
